This is the BEST game I've EVER played with my two boys, aged 7 and 9. A+++++ 11/10, best ever. Together we've learned about physics, gravity, centre of mass, flight, ballast, geometery, engineering, problem solving, and other great topics. As a bonus is it probably the first game my wife has shown any interest in too! It's also sparked more interest in the kids toward real-life building, and they've dusted off their lego and are often inspired to build in real life after playing.
In the course of 'beating' the first island we built a number of tanks with progressively better steering and durabily, a couple flying machines including a kamakazee model, a crane, a couple cars, and a number of mostly useless but fun "prototypes." Awsome.
I've found many games like this have been too complicated or been burdened by a cumbersome UI. This game perfectly strikes the balance between simplicity and complexity. The game mechanics are deep enough to stay very interesting for a long time, and simple enough that we've never been frustrated. I really hope the devs stick to this winning formula they have here and just work on content, refinements, and more building pieces.

So, Besiege. This is a really unique game, and I'd really recommend it to a lot of people. If you're deciding whether or not to buy this game, just spend 5 minutes on reading this review.

[h1]Who should buy this game[/h1]
[list]
    [*]People, who look forward to playing a very fun physics-based sandbox game
    [*]Gamers, who are interested in some kind of technic and war contraptions
    [*]The creative ones, people who can find a thousand solutions to one task
[/list]

[h1]Why should I buy Besiege?[/h1]
[olist]
    [*]It's growing very quickly and is not abandoned, unlike a lot of Early Access games
    [*]Very cheap as for the content that it gives you
    [*]Enjoyable gameplay and graphics
    [*]A ton of space for creativity
    [*]The developers promised to add a [b]multiplayer mode[/b] and a multiplayer level editor in late 2017!
[/olist]
Below is a more detailed breakdown.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay is the main point of Besiege. Just to list a few things off, this game provides you with a nice campaign (even though there are not so many levels yet, but every level has a ton of replayability potential). There are also a couple of sandbox maps. The player is equipped with infinite amounts of different varieties of building blocks and elements. There is literally everything, starting with a simple cube and going right to holders, pistons, different versions of cannons, bombs, wings and a lot of other stuff. The best thing is that anything you will build will work and people have already came up with some really crazy ideas. Ever wanted to create a huge flying carrier? Or a machine that swings a giant hammer around itself, smashing everything to pieces? You can basically do that. Also, slow-motion is epic.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
I like the graphics. There is not much to say, but the visual style is pretty unique and is just enjoyable. Fire, water, explosions, the machines themselves look great and organic.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There is some nice ambient music that I really enjoy listening to. The sounds produced by machines and structures are simply great.

[h1]Sanbox-iness[/h1]
This is not some kind of an official criteria, but I just wanted to mention how flexible Besiege really is. First off, in any level (including the campaign ones), you are able to disable the small building box that limits you and build anything. The sky is the limit (and your computers hardware, of course). There are quite a few cheats on the options panel, that can give you something like zero gravity or infinite ammo (most of the weapons fire only once or just can be held on for around 10 seconds). There are 3 large sandbox levels. And, as I've already mentioned, a level editor and a full multiplayer system are coming in 2017 (well, hopefully in 2017. The devs promised at least.)

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
As for a sandbox fan, it's pretty much a 10/10. I would rate is as the best "wait, did this just [b]really[/b] work?" simulator.

I've played this game for so long I followed its development on imgur like half a decade ago. Besiege is really one of the first of its kind - a game about building vehicles to meet the demands of the mission at hand. Before Simple Planes or Trailmakers, there was Besiege. The game really just gives you a tool box full of blocks, motors, spikes, and bombs and asks you to complete deceptively simple missions. The fun of the game comes from what you decide to do to solve the problem at hand. Technically, a helicopter with a grabber and a bomb can finish like 4/5ths of the original campaign, but the real meat and potatoes of the game comes from building inefficient, unoptimized solutions. If you have an inkling of a creative bone in your body, this is the game for you. The building mechanics are solid, the gameplay loop is fun, the game is graphically pretty good for an indie title, and the sound design of the game is memorable. The performance is pretty good considering the physics at play and the degree to which you can crank the graphical fidelity. If you like building solutions to problems, this is a fun game to pick up!

If you’ve ever wanted a game where you can slap wheels, blades, springs, rockets, cannons, and a suspicious amount of spinning parts together and somehow call it “engineering,” this is the game for you. Besiege gives you an incredibly flexible building system that lets you create anything from a janky one block buggy to a full blown mechanical dragon or flying death machine. The physics are great, the destruction is satisfying, and the medieval toybox aesthetic fits the tone perfectly.

The campaign is… decent. Fun at first, but it definitely drags in the later levels. The difficulty ramps up while the objectives don’t really evolve, so you end up spending way too long fine tuning a machine for a single stage only to scrap it entirely because the next mission needs something completely different. It’s not bad, just repetitive, and a lot of players (myself included) find themselves losing interest before the end. But honestly, the real magic of Besiege is the sandbox. It’s where the game truly comes alive. You can build whatever monstrosity your imagination can conjure, test it, blow it up, rebuild it, and repeat the cycle endlessly. A lot of players treat it like a creative workshop recreating real world vehicles, making functional logic machines, designing massive siege engines, or just building the dumbest contraption possible to see if it flies (it won’t, but that’s half the fun).

Performance is surprisingly solid considering the level of chaos you can unleash, though heavier builds can still choke your framerate into the dirt pretty much expected at this point. The Workshop support is also fantastic, with thousands of machines ready to download if you ever hit a creative block. Even if you skip the campaign entirely, Besiege is still a blast. It’s the kind of game you install for “a quick session,” play for three hours straight, and suddenly you’re trying to build a fire-breathing tank that can also fold into a walking robot. It’s creative, chaotic, and endlessly entertaining.

I believe that I've owned this game for about 5 years at this point, maybe longer. I got it shortly after it was released on Early Access. It's not really a game that I come back to often, mostly only when I have a random idea or want to mess around with some mechanical things. However, each time that I come back, there's usually something new.

After some time of playing vanilla and I started to get bored of it, I learned about modding. The modding community was great and there were many cool mods. From there, Spiderling then adapted some of those mods into the game, most notably the advanced building mod not too long ago. This enabled me to build even more things without having to set up complex mods.

It's clear that the developers care a lot about the community, but they don't try to force it down your throat with random DLCs or updates. They simply fix bugs and implement user feedback in constructive ways. 

While I do think the difficulty of advanced building techniques is exponential, it's not so difficult that it's impossible to do anything. The original campaign only requires simple designs and you have a lot of creative freedom. 

Therefore, while you may not be hand-held on a lot of things, it's simple enough to be very rewarding, even if you don't get it on the first try. You can get a lot of feedback on the designs you make because of the level design.

On the flip side of simple designs, the things people can create in this game is mind-blowing from a complexity standpoint. There are some really smart and talented people that have figured out the quirks of this game to create mind-blowing designs. Not to mention, you can write mods in C#. I haven't done it, but I'm certainly interested to see what is possible.

I can see myself playing this game in 30+ years, assuming my hardware supports it. I still can't believe I managed 400+ hours in the game so far.

Ahhh Besiege, A game that was there in my darkest of days, It's a simple concept where you are given basic parts or programmable stuff and such and given practically unlimited freedom to do whatever the hell you can think of with said parts, so long as they can complete an objective like carrying a crate or destroying a floating castle. Although nobody said you HAVE to do those objectives, given some steering hinges for a car? Nah use them to create a giant transforming truck or even the basis of a giant crossbow. Besiege is one of those games where they expect you to do something simple, yet they encourage and support insane complexity!

This game has captured me time and time again, it's such a simple yet amazingly complex little 'Tinker Toy' 
that i've always found myself coming back to over the years, be it to mess around with war machines, prototype mechanisms for IRL projects, or simply to screw about with ""loving and caring for""(killing) chickens, it's always drawn me back, and I love it!

The game itself is just a physics sandbox alpha as is, yet the gameplay and fun one can have from this is endless. Really the fun is up to your creativity as that is your limit, and for 7$ there's no reason you shouldn't get this game.

To be truthful, I didn't expect much from this game at all.  I'm rather sceptical of any game that's available under early access.  As it happened, I bought this once it made full release.  Still didn't expect much of it... but pleased to say I've been proven wrong.

There's a very simple aim - build machines to defeat the levels.  But that's hardly the point to the game.  Really it just gives you tools to build what you want to do what you want.  The people most likely to get most out of this game are those interested in engineering.  

Me ?  I'm not an engineer - I just thought it looked like it could be fun.  Which it has been.  I'm about 90 hours into this game now.  Beat all the zones long ago.  Now just tinkering with designs or even looking at new ways to beat a level.  Still learning.  Still having fun.
